### Quantitative PCR (qPCR)
The RaPure Total RNA Kit (Magen, R4011-02) was employed to extract total cellular and tissue RNA, following the manufacturer’s instructions. Genomic DNA was digested, and RNase-free water was applied to elute RNA. The purified RNA was used for cDNA synthesis using All-in-One First-Strand SuperMix containing dsDNase (Nuoyang Biotech, EG15133S). qPCR was performed using ChamQ SYBR Color qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Q431-02) on a QuantStudio 3 system (ThermoFisher, A28573 ). Relative targeted gene expression was determined based on the 2 –ΔΔCt method, normalizing to 18S. The primers used for qPCR are listed in Table 2 .

### RNA-seq and data analysis
Total RNA was extracted and purified from OA-treated HepG2 cells (shNC or shMETTL7A) using the method described above. For library preparation, 1 µg of RNA per sample was processed with the NEBNext® Ultra™ RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina® (New England Biolabs) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA fragment selection and purification were performed using the AMPure XP system (Beckman Coulter), and library quality was evaluated with the Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100. Clustering of index-coded libraries was carried out on the cBot Cluster Generation System using the TruSeq PE Cluster Kit v3-cBot-HS (Illumina). Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq platform to generate 150 bp paired-end reads. Three independent biological replicates were performed and analyzed for each experimental condition.

### METTL7A expression is upregulated in an MASLD/NAFLD cellular model
To investigate the potential role of METTL7A in MASLD/NAFLD, we first optimized the in vitro steatosis model conditions using a concentration gradient of OA. HepG2 and Huh7 cells were treated with various concentrations of OA for 24 h, and cell viability was evaluated using MTT assays. Based on the cell viability results and the efficiency of intracellular lipid deposition assessed by Oil Red O staining, optimal and non-toxic concentrations of 1 mM for HepG2 cells and 200 μM for Huh7 cells were selected for subsequent experiments, which align with widely used protocols to induce lipid accumulation 23 , 24 . Huh7 cells exhibited cytotoxicity above 200 μM, whereas HepG2 cells maintained high viability up to 1 mM. Both cell lines displayed marked intracellular lipid deposition as detected by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 1 A, B). qPCR and Western blotting revealed significant increases in METTL7A mRNA and protein levels in OA-treated HCC cells compared with controls (Fig. 1 C, D). These results suggest that METTL7A may contribute to lipid accumulation in hepatocytes.

### METTL7A knockdown mitigates lipid accumulation in OA-treated HCC cells
To define METTL7A’s function in hepatic lipid metabolism, we generated three METTL7A-targeting shRNAs. qPCR analysis in HEK293T cells showed effective knockdown by all constructs, with shMETTL7A-1 achieving the greatest suppression (Fig. 2 A); thus, it was selected for further experiments. In both HepG2 and Huh7 cells, METTL7A depletion markedly reduced OA-induced lipid accumulation as shown by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 2 B). MTT assays showed that METTL7A silencing partially rescued the OA-induced decrease in cell viability (Fig. 2 C). Consistent with reduced lipid accumulation, METTL7A knockdown significantly lowered LDL-C, TG, and TC levels while increasing HDL-C in OA-treated cells (Fig. 2 D). At the molecular scale, METTL7A depletion was confirmed by qPCR and Western blotting (Fig. 3 A, B). Moreover, METTL7A deficiency downregulated ACC and FAS expression while upregulating HSL in OA-treated hepatocytes (Fig. 3 B). These findings indicate that METTL7A acts as a positive regulator of lipid accumulation.
METTL7A knockdown reduces lipid accumulation and improves cell viability in OA-treated hepatocytes. ( A ) qPCR validation of three METTL7A-targeting shRNAs in HEK293T cells, identifying shMETTL7A-1 as the most effective construct. ( B ) Oil Red O staining of HepG2 and Huh7 cells with or without METTL7A knockdown following OA treatment. Lipid droplet areas was performed using ImageJ software. ( C ) MTT assay showing that METTL7A depletion partially rescues OA-induced reduction in cell viability. ( D ) Biochemical measurements of LDL-C, TG, TC, and HDL-C levels in control and OA-treated cells with or without METTL7A silencing. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test was used for P-value calculation. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3). Fig. 3.

### Depletion of METTL7A causes reduced expression of PLIN5 and blocks the activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway
To delineate the mechanism by which METTL7A promotes lipid deposition in OA-treated HCC cells, we performed RNA-seq using control and METTL7A-deficient HepG2 cells exposed to OA for 24 h. Among the DEGs, PLIN5 attracted our attention due to its known function in hepatic lipid metabolism. qPCR and Western blotting validated the RNA-seq data, showing that PLIN5 expression was greatly decreased in OA-treated METTL7A-deficient HCC cells. Notably, PLIN5 expression was also strongly induced by OA treatment, similar to METTL7A (Fig. 4 A and B). We also investigated the activation of PI3K/AKT pathway, a key player in hepatic lipid metabolism. Western blotting indicated that the phosphorylation of PI3K and AKT (P-PI3K and P-AKT), which represents activation of the pathway, was enhanced by OA in both cell lines; however, this effect was nullified by METTL7A depletion (Fig. 4 C). These observations demonstrate that METTL7A facilitates lipid accumulation in the hepatocytes by inducing PLIN5 and the PI3K/AKT pathway.

### METTL7A interacts with SAPCD2 in HCC cells
To further explore how METTL7A regulates PLIN5 and PI3K/AKT signaling, a preliminary MS screening was initially performed as an exploratory approach using control and Flag-METTL7A–expressing HepG2 cells, with candidates cross-referenced against PLIN5 interactors in BioGRID 25 . Among the candidates, SAPCD2 emerged as a candidate of interest (Fig. 5 A) because it is also reported to activate PI3K/AKT signaling 26 . Coomassie blue staining of proteins pulled down by IP revealed a potential band corresponding to SAPCD2 (Fig. 5 B). Exogenous co-IP assays verified the interaction between overexpressed METTL7A and SAPCD2 in HepG2 and Huh7 cells (Fig. 5 C). Furthermore, endogenous co-IP assays confirmed that native METTL7A physically interacts with endogenous SAPCD2 under physiological conditions in HepG2 and Huh7 cells (Fig. 5 D). Additionally, qPCR and Western blotting revealed that METTL7A-deficient HepG2 and Huh7 cells exhibited significantly reduced SAPCD2 expression (Fig. 5 E and F). These findings suggest that METTL7A may regulate PLIN5 expression and PI3K/AKT activation in hepatocytes through SAPCD2.

### SAPCD2 is required for OA-induced PI3K/AKT activation and PLIN5 expression
To define the functional role of SAPCD2, we first validated its knockdown and overexpression efficiencies in hepatocytes (Fig. 6 A, B). Western blotting revealed that OA stimulation significantly upregulated METTL7A, SAPCD2, and PLIN5 expression, alongside increased PI3K and AKT phosphorylation. SAPCD2 silencing suppressed OA-induced p-PI3K and p-AKT levels and abolished PLIN5 upregulation without altering METTL7A (Fig. 6 C, D). Conversely, SAPCD2 overexpression further enhanced PI3K/AKT phosphorylation and PLIN5 expression (Fig. 6 C, D). Consistent with these molecular changes, Oil Red O staining demonstrated that SAPCD2 knockdown significantly attenuated OA-induced intracellular lipid accumulation, whereas SAPCD2 overexpression further exacerbated lipid droplet deposition in both cell lines (Fig. 6 E). These results indicate that SAPCD2 acts downstream of METTL7A to mediate OA-induced PI3K/AKT activation and PLIN5 expression.

### Overexpression of SAPCD2 rescues lipid accumulation in OA-treated HCC cells with METTL7A deficiency
To evaluate whether SAPCD2 mediates the lipogenic effects of METTL7A, we overexpressed SAPCD2 in METTL7A-deficient HepG2 and Huh7 cells. SAPCD2 overexpression restored lipid accumulation in OA-treated METTL7A-knockdown cells, as shown by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 7 A). MTT assays indicated that cell viability decreased upon SAPCD2 overexpression in METTL7A-deficient, OA-treated cells (Fig. 7 B). Furthermore, SAPCD2-overexpressing METTL7A-deficient HCC cells expressed higher levels of LDL-C, TG, and TC, along with lower levels of HDL-C (Fig. 7 C). Additionally, qPCR and Western blotting uncovered that overexpression of SAPCD2 significantly increased the expression of PLIN5 in OA-induced METTL7A-deficient HCC cells (Fig. 8 A and B). qPCR also showed that SAPCD2 overexpression led to downregulated levels of HSL and upregulated expression of FAS and ACC (Fig. 8 A). Western blotting indicated that the PI3K/AKT pathway activation was enhanced by excessive SAPCD2 in METTL7A-deficient HCC cells exposed to OA (Fig. 8 B). These data suggest that SAPCD2 is a critical mediator of METTL7A’s role in promoting lipogenesis in OA-treated HCC cells.
SAPCD2 overexpression rescues lipid accumulation in METTL7A-deficient HCC cells. ( A ) Oil Red O staining showing upregulation of lipid accumulation in METTL7A-knockdown HepG2 and Huh7 cells upon SAPCD2 overexpression. Lipid droplet areas was performed using ImageJ software. ( B ) MTT assay showing reduced cell viability when SAPCD2 is overexpressed in METTL7A-deficient, OA-treated cells. ( C ) Biochemical analysis demonstrating increased LDL-C, TG, and TC and decreased HDL-C after SAPCD2 overexpression. One-way ANOVA and Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test were utilized for P -value calculation. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3). Fig. 8.

### METTL7A knockdown alleviates HFD-induced hepatic steatosis in MASLD/NAFLD mice
To validate these findings in vivo, we established a mouse model of MASLD/NAFLD and infected the mice with AAV carrying shNC or shMETTL7A. Compared to the control group, livers from the Model and Model + shNC groups appeared pale, consistent with steatosis, whereas the Model + shMETTL7A group exhibited darker liver coloration, suggesting reduced lipid content (Fig. 9 A). Histological analysis using H&amp;E and Oil Red O staining confirmed that METTL7A knockdown substantially attenuated steatosis (Fig. 9 B and C). Biochemical assays revealed elevated LDL-C, TC, TG, AST, and ALT and reduced HDL-C in the Model and Model + shNC groups, all of which were partially normalized by METTL7A knockdown (Fig. 9 D). qPCR and Western blotting verified efficient METTL7A knockdown in the liver (Fig. 9 E and F). Expression of PLIN5, SAPCD2, FAS, and ACC was reduced, while HSL levels increased upon METTL7A silencing (Fig. 9 E and F). PI3K/AKT activation, elevated in the Model and Model + shNC groups, was markedly suppressed in METTL7A-deficient livers (Fig. 9 F). Collectively, these results demonstrate that METTL7A promotes hepatic lipid accumulation.

### Discussion
In this study, we identify METTL7A as a previously unrecognized regulator of hepatic lipid metabolism and MASLD/NAFLD progression. Although METTL7A is known as an m 6 A RNA methyltransferase implicated in cancer biology and also functions as a thiol methyltransferase in the liver, playing an essential role in drug metabolism, its metabolic functions in hepatocytes have remained unclear. Our findings demonstrate that METTL7A expression is markedly elevated during hepatocellular lipid loading and that METTL7A actively drives steatosis both in vitro and in vivo. These results broaden our understanding of METTL7A’s role in liver physiology.
The mechanism by which lipid accumulation induces METTL7A overexpression in hepatocytes remains unknown. Previous studies show that METTL7A mRNA expression is regulated by several noncoding RNAs, including miR-6807-5p, LINC01123, miR-654-5p, and miR-27a, across different biological contexts 27 – 29 . Notably, these noncoding RNAs also modulate hepatic lipid metabolism and MASLD/NAFLD 30 , 31 , raising the possibility that they may regulate steatosis by targeting METTL7A. Additionally, METTL7A transcription can be influenced by DNA methylation 32 , but whether this mechanism contributes to its increased expression under steatotic conditions remains to be clarified. Importantly, validation of METTL7A upregulation in liver tissues from MASLD/NAFLD patients will strengthen its clinical relevance.
To elucidate the mechanism underlying METTL7A’s lipogenic function in hepatocytes, we performed transcriptomic analyses and identified PLIN5 as a key candidate. PLIN5 is a central regulator of intracellular lipid metabolism, essential for lipid storage and oxidation 33 – 35 . Consistent with METTL7A’s pro-lipogenic role, PLIN5 knockout mice exhibit impaired lipid accumulation in the heart and skeletal muscle and show resistance to MASLD/NAFLD and HCC, whereas PLIN5 overexpression induces cardiac steatosis 20 , 35 . ### Abstract
Methyltransferase-like protein 7A (METTL7A), an m 6 A RNA methyltransferase and thiol methyltransferase enriched in hepatocytes, has been implicated in cancer biology, yet its role in hepatic lipid metabolism and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD) remains unknown. Hepatic steatosis was induced in HepG2 and Huh7 cells using oleic acid (OA). The role of METTL7A was examined through shRNA-mediated knockdown, RNA sequencing, lipid metabolic assays, and rescue experiments. Protein interactions were assessed via mass spectrometry and co-immunoprecipitation. An AAV-shMETTL7A mouse MASLD/NAFLD model was used to validate in vivo relevance. METTL7A expression was significantly upregulated in OA-induced steatotic hepatocytes. METTL7A silencing mitigated lipid accumulation, improved cell viability, reduced LDL-C, TC, and TG levels, and restored HDL-C. Transcriptomic profiling identified PLIN5 as a key downstream target reduced upon METTL7A depletion. Mechanistically, METTL7A knockdown inhibited PI3K/AKT activation and suppressed PLIN5 expression. Mass spectrometry revealed SAPCD2 as a METTL7A-interacting protein, and SAPCD2 overexpression restored lipid accumulation, PI3K/AKT activation, and PLIN5 levels in METTL7A-deficient cells. In vivo, AAV-mediated METTL7A knockdown alleviated hepatic steatosis, normalized serum lipid profiles and liver injury markers, and reduced SAPCD2, PLIN5, FAS, and ACC while increasing HSL expression. METTL7A is a previously unrecognized regulator of hepatic lipid homeostasis that promotes steatosis by sustaining SAPCD2 expression and activating the PI3K/AKT pathway and PLIN5 expression. Targeting METTL7A may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for MASLD/NAFLD.

### Introduction
Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly named nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) refers to a wide range of liver conditions marked by abnormal fat deposition in hepatocytes among individuals who drink little or no alcohol 1 . It has become one of the most prevalent chronic liver disorders worldwide, strongly associated with metabolic dysfunction and affecting roughly 30% of the global population 2 . MASLD/NAFLD is generally classified into two forms: metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver/nonalcoholic fatty liver (MAFL/NAFL) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis/nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (MASH/NASH) 3 . MAFL/NAFL involves simple steatosis without notable inflammation or fibrosis and is often viewed as relatively mild, though progression can occur. In contrast, MASH/NASH features steatosis accompanied by inflammation and hepatocellular damage, which may advance to fibrosis, cirrhosis, or even hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) 3 , 4 .
Key contributors to MASLD/NAFLD include obesity, type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, hypertension, dyslipidemia, genetic susceptibility, and unhealthy lifestyle habits 5 , 6 . At present, few medications have been approved in the United States specifically for MASLD/NAFLD or MASH/NASH therapy 5 , 7 . Current management focuses on reducing excess weight through lifestyle modification, pharmacologic therapy, or bariatric and endoscopic procedures, and correcting metabolic abnormalities 8 , 9 . Therefore, a deeper understanding of the molecular pathways driving hepatic lipid accumulation is urgently needed for novel therapy development.
Hepatic steatosis develops when lipid acquisition exceeds lipid disposal—that is, when fatty acid uptake and de novo lipogenesis outpace fatty acid oxidation and lipid export. In MASLD/NAFLD, both hepatic fatty acid uptake and lipogenesis are elevated, whereas the compensatory increase in fatty acid oxidation is insufficient to normalize lipid le

### Plasmid construction
To overexpress METTL7A or SAPCD2, their coding sequence was respectively ligated into the pECMV-3 × FLAG or pLVX-CMV-HA-pGK-puro backbone. The resulting vector was named Flag-METTL7A or SAPCD2 OE. In order to deplete METTL7A, its targeting shRNAs were inserted into the pLKO.1-puro backbone. Three shMETTL7A constructs were produced: shMETTL7A-1, shMETTL7A-2, and shMETTL7A-3. A non-specific shRNA (shNC) was constructed to function as a control. All the resulting plasmids were subjected to Sanger sequencing to ensure sequence accuracy before being used for functional assays. Table 1 shows the details of primers. Plasmid transfection was performed using Lipofectamine® 2000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11668-019) when cells reached 70–80% confluence.

### Quantitative PCR (qPCR)
The RaPure Total RNA Kit (Magen, R4011-02) was employed to extract total cellular and tissue RNA, following the manufacturer’s instructions. Genomic DNA was digested, and RNase-free water was applied to elute RNA. The purified RNA was used for cDNA synthesis using All-in-One First-Strand SuperMix containing dsDNase (Nuoyang Biotech, EG15133S). qPCR was performed using ChamQ SYBR Color qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Q431-02) on a QuantStudio 3 system (ThermoFisher, A28573 ). Relative targeted gene expression was determined based on the 2 –ΔΔCt method, normalizing to 18S. The primers used for qPCR are listed in Table 2 .

### RNA-seq and data analysis
Total RNA was extracted and purified from OA-treated HepG2 cells (shNC or shMETTL7A) using the method described above. For library preparation, 1 µg of RNA per sample was processed with the NEBNext® Ultra™ RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina® (New England Biolabs) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA fragment selection and purification were performed using the AMPure XP system (Beckman Coulter), and library quality was evaluated with the Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100. Clustering of index-coded libraries was carried out on the cBot Cluster Generation System using the TruSeq PE Cluster Kit v3-cBot-HS (Illumina). Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq platform to generate 150 bp paired-end reads. Three independent biological replicates were performed and analyzed for each experimental condition.

### METTL7A expression is upregulated in an MASLD/NAFLD cellular model
To investigate the potential role of METTL7A in MASLD/NAFLD, we first optimized the in vitro steatosis model conditions using a concentration gradient of OA. HepG2 and Huh7 cells were treated with various concentrations of OA for 24 h, and cell viability was evaluated using MTT assays. Based on the cell viability results and the efficiency of intracellular lipid deposition assessed by Oil Red O staining, optimal and non-toxic concentrations of 1 mM for HepG2 cells and 200 μM for Huh7 cells were selected for subsequent experiments, which align with widely used protocols to induce lipid accumulation 23 , 24 . Huh7 cells exhibited cytotoxicity above 200 μM, whereas HepG2 cells maintained high viability up to 1 mM. Both cell lines displayed marked intracellular lipid deposition as detected by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 1 A, B). qPCR and Western blotting revealed significant increases in METTL7A mRNA and protein levels in OA-treated HCC cells compared with controls (Fig. 1 C, D). These results suggest that METTL7A may contribute to lipid accumulation in hepatocytes.

### METTL7A knockdown mitigates lipid accumulation in OA-treated HCC cells
To define METTL7A’s function in hepatic lipid metabolism, we generated three METTL7A-targeting shRNAs. qPCR analysis in HEK293T cells showed effective knockdown by all constructs, with shMETTL7A-1 achieving the greatest suppression (Fig. 2 A); thus, it was selected for further experiments. In both HepG2 and Huh7 cells, METTL7A depletion markedly reduced OA-induced lipid accumulation as shown by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 2 B). MTT assays showed that METTL7A silencing partially rescued the OA-induced decrease in cell viability (Fig. 2 C). Consistent with reduced lipid accumulation, METTL7A knockdown significantly lowered LDL-C, TG, and TC levels while increasing HDL-C in OA-treated cells (Fig. 2 D). At the molecular scale, METTL7A depletion was confirmed by qPCR and Western blotting (Fig. 3 A, B). Moreover, METTL7A deficiency downregulated ACC and FAS expression while upregulating HSL in OA-treated hepatocytes (Fig. 3 B). These findings indicate that METTL7A acts as a positive regulator of lipid accumulation.
METTL7A knockdown reduces lipid accumulation and improves cell viability in OA-treated hepatocytes. ( A ) qPCR validation of three METTL7A-targeting shRNAs in HEK293T cells, identifying shMETTL7A-1 as the most effective construct. ( B ) Oil Red O staining of HepG2 and Huh7 cells with or without METTL7A knockdown following OA treatment. Lipid droplet areas was performed using ImageJ software. ( C ) MTT assay showing that METTL7A depletion partially rescues OA-induced reduction in cell viability. ( D ) Biochemical measurements of LDL-C, TG, TC, and HDL-C levels in control and OA-treated cells with or without METTL7A silencing. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test was used for P-value calculation. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3). Fig. 3.

### Depletion of METTL7A causes reduced expression of PLIN5 and blocks the activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway
To delineate the mechanism by which METTL7A promotes lipid deposition in OA-treated HCC cells, we performed RNA-seq using control and METTL7A-deficient HepG2 cells exposed to OA for 24 h. Among the DEGs, PLIN5 attracted our attention due to its known function in hepatic lipid metabolism. qPCR and Western blotting validated the RNA-seq data, showing that PLIN5 expression was greatly decreased in OA-treated METTL7A-deficient HCC cells. Notably, PLIN5 expression was also strongly induced by OA treatment, similar to METTL7A (Fig. 4 A and B). We also investigated the activation of PI3K/AKT pathway, a key player in hepatic lipid metabolism. Western blotting indicated that the phosphorylation of PI3K and AKT (P-PI3K and P-AKT), which represents activation of the pathway, was enhanced by OA in both cell lines; however, this effect was nullified by METTL7A depletion (Fig. 4 C). These observations demonstrate that METTL7A facilitates lipid accumulation in the hepatocytes by inducing PLIN5 and the PI3K/AKT pathway.

### METTL7A interacts with SAPCD2 in HCC cells
To further explore how METTL7A regulates PLIN5 and PI3K/AKT signaling, a preliminary MS screening was initially performed as an exploratory approach using control and Flag-METTL7A–expressing HepG2 cells, with candidates cross-referenced against PLIN5 interactors in BioGRID 25 . Among the candidates, SAPCD2 emerged as a candidate of interest (Fig. 5 A) because it is also reported to activate PI3K/AKT signaling 26 . Coomassie blue staining of proteins pulled down by IP revealed a potential band corresponding to SAPCD2 (Fig. 5 B). Exogenous co-IP assays verified the interaction between overexpressed METTL7A and SAPCD2 in HepG2 and Huh7 cells (Fig. 5 C). Furthermore, endogenous co-IP assays confirmed that native METTL7A physically interacts with endogenous SAPCD2 under physiological conditions in HepG2 and Huh7 cells (Fig. 5 D). Additionally, qPCR and Western blotting revealed that METTL7A-deficient HepG2 and Huh7 cells exhibited significantly reduced SAPCD2 expression (Fig. 5 E and F). These findings suggest that METTL7A may regulate PLIN5 expression and PI3K/AKT activation in hepatocytes through SAPCD2.

### SAPCD2 is required for OA-induced PI3K/AKT activation and PLIN5 expression
To define the functional role of SAPCD2, we first validated its knockdown and overexpression efficiencies in hepatocytes (Fig. 6 A, B). Western blotting revealed that OA stimulation significantly upregulated METTL7A, SAPCD2, and PLIN5 expression, alongside increased PI3K and AKT phosphorylation. SAPCD2 silencing suppressed OA-induced p-PI3K and p-AKT levels and abolished PLIN5 upregulation without altering METTL7A (Fig. 6 C, D). Conversely, SAPCD2 overexpression further enhanced PI3K/AKT phosphorylation and PLIN5 expression (Fig. 6 C, D). Consistent with these molecular changes, Oil Red O staining demonstrated that SAPCD2 knockdown significantly attenuated OA-induced intracellular lipid accumulation, whereas SAPCD2 overexpression further exacerbated lipid droplet deposition in both cell lines (Fig. 6 E). These results indicate that SAPCD2 acts downstream of METTL7A to mediate OA-induced PI3K/AKT activation and PLIN5 expression.

### Overexpression of SAPCD2 rescues lipid accumulation in OA-treated HCC cells with METTL7A deficiency
To evaluate whether SAPCD2 mediates the lipogenic effects of METTL7A, we overexpressed SAPCD2 in METTL7A-deficient HepG2 and Huh7 cells. SAPCD2 overexpression restored lipid accumulation in OA-treated METTL7A-knockdown cells, as shown by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 7 A). MTT assays indicated that cell viability decreased upon SAPCD2 overexpression in METTL7A-deficient, OA-treated cells (Fig. 7 B). Furthermore, SAPCD2-overexpressing METTL7A-deficient HCC cells expressed higher levels of LDL-C, TG, and TC, along with lower levels of HDL-C (Fig. 7 C). Additionally, qPCR and Western blotting uncovered that overexpression of SAPCD2 significantly increased the expression of PLIN5 in OA-induced METTL7A-deficient HCC cells (Fig. 8 A and B). qPCR also showed that SAPCD2 overexpression led to downregulated levels of HSL and upregulated expression of FAS and ACC (Fig. 8 A). Western blotting indicated that the PI3K/AKT pathway activation was enhanced by excessive SAPCD2 in METTL7A-deficient HCC cells exposed to OA (Fig. 8 B). These data suggest that SAPCD2 is a critical mediator of METTL7A’s role in promoting lipogenesis in OA-treated HCC cells.
SAPCD2 overexpression rescues lipid accumulation in METTL7A-deficient HCC cells. ( A ) Oil Red O staining showing upregulation of lipid accumulation in METTL7A-knockdown HepG2 and Huh7 cells upon SAPCD2 overexpression. Lipid droplet areas was performed using ImageJ software. ( B ) MTT assay showing reduced cell viability when SAPCD2 is overexpressed in METTL7A-deficient, OA-treated cells. ( C ) Biochemical analysis demonstrating increased LDL-C, TG, and TC and decreased HDL-C after SAPCD2 overexpression. One-way ANOVA and Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test were utilized for P -value calculation. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3). Fig. 8.

### METTL7A knockdown alleviates HFD-induced hepatic steatosis in MASLD/NAFLD mice
To validate these findings in vivo, we established a mouse model of MASLD/NAFLD and infected the mice with AAV carrying shNC or shMETTL7A. Compared to the control group, livers from the Model and Model + shNC groups appeared pale, consistent with steatosis, whereas the Model + shMETTL7A group exhibited darker liver coloration, suggesting reduced lipid content (Fig. 9 A). Histological analysis using H&amp;E and Oil Red O staining confirmed that METTL7A knockdown substantially attenuated steatosis (Fig. 9 B and C). Biochemical assays revealed elevated LDL-C, TC, TG, AST, and ALT and reduced HDL-C in the Model and Model + shNC groups, all of which were partially normalized by METTL7A knockdown (Fig. 9 D). qPCR and Western blotting verified efficient METTL7A knockdown in the liver (Fig. 9 E and F). Expression of PLIN5, SAPCD2, FAS, and ACC was reduced, while HSL levels increased upon METTL7A silencing (Fig. 9 E and F). PI3K/AKT activation, elevated in the Model and Model + shNC groups, was markedly suppressed in METTL7A-deficient livers (Fig. 9 F). Collectively, these results demonstrate that METTL7A promotes hepatic lipid accumulation.

### Discussion
In this study, we identify METTL7A as a previously unrecognized regulator of hepatic lipid metabolism and MASLD/NAFLD progression. Although METTL7A is known as an m 6 A RNA methyltransferase implicated in cancer biology and also functions as a thiol methyltransferase in the liver, playing an essential role in drug metabolism, its metabolic functions in hepatocytes have remained unclear. Our findings demonstrate that METTL7A expression is markedly elevated during hepatocellular lipid loading and that METTL7A actively drives steatosis both in vitro and in vivo. These results broaden our understanding of METTL7A’s role in liver physiology.
The mechanism by which lipid accumulation induces METTL7A overexpression in hepatocytes remains unknown. Previous studies show that METTL7A mRNA expression is regulated by several noncoding RNAs, including miR-6807-5p, LINC01123, miR-654-5p, and miR-27a, across different biological contexts 27 – 29 . Notably, these noncoding RNAs also modulate hepatic lipid metabolism and MASLD/NAFLD 30 , 31 , raising the possibility that they may regulate steatosis by targeting METTL7A. Additionally, METTL7A transcription can be influenced by DNA methylation 32 , but whether this mechanism contributes to its increased expression under steatotic conditions remains to be clarified. Importantly, validation of METTL7A upregulation in liver tissues from MASLD/NAFLD patients will strengthen its clinical relevance.
To elucidate the mechanism underlying METTL7A’s lipogenic function in hepatocytes, we performed transcriptomic analyses and identified PLIN5 as a key candidate. PLIN5 is a central regulator of intracellular lipid metabolism, essential for lipid storage and oxidation 33 – 35 . Consistent with METTL7A’s pro-lipogenic role, PLIN5 knockout mice exhibit impaired lipid accumulation in the heart and skeletal muscle and show resistance to MASLD/NAFLD and HCC, whereas PLIN5 overexpression induces cardiac steatosis 20 , 35 . ### Abstract
Methyltransferase-like protein 7A (METTL7A), an m 6 A RNA methyltransferase and thiol methyltransferase enriched in hepatocytes, has been implicated in cancer biology, yet its role in hepatic lipid metabolism and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD) remains unknown. Hepatic steatosis was induced in HepG2 and Huh7 cells using oleic acid (OA). The role of METTL7A was examined through shRNA-mediated knockdown, RNA sequencing, lipid metabolic assays, and rescue experiments. Protein interactions were assessed via mass spectrometry and co-immunoprecipitation. An AAV-shMETTL7A mouse MASLD/NAFLD model was used to validate in vivo relevance. METTL7A expression was significantly upregulated in OA-induced steatotic hepatocytes. METTL7A silencing mitigated lipid accumulation, improved cell viability, reduced LDL-C, TC, and TG levels, and restored HDL-C. Transcriptomic profiling identified PLIN5 as a key downstream target reduced upon METTL7A depletion. Mechanistically, METTL7A knockdown inhibited PI3K/AKT activation and suppressed PLIN5 expression. Mass spectrometry revealed SAPCD2 as a METTL7A-interacting protein, and SAPCD2 overexpression restored lipid accumulation, PI3K/AKT activation, and PLIN5 levels in METTL7A-deficient cells. In vivo, AAV-mediated METTL7A knockdown alleviated hepatic steatosis, normalized serum lipid profiles and liver injury markers, and reduced SAPCD2, PLIN5, FAS, and ACC while increasing HSL expression. METTL7A is a previously unrecognized regulator of hepatic lipid homeostasis that promotes steatosis by sustaining SAPCD2 expression and activating the PI3K/AKT pathway and PLIN5 expression. Targeting METTL7A may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for MASLD/NAFLD.

### Introduction
Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly named nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) refers to a wide range of liver conditions marked by abnormal fat deposition in hepatocytes among individuals who drink little or no alcohol 1 . It has become one of the most prevalent chronic liver disorders worldwide, strongly associated with metabolic dysfunction and affecting roughly 30% of the global population 2 . MASLD/NAFLD is generally classified into two forms: metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver/nonalcoholic fatty liver (MAFL/NAFL) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis/nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (MASH/NASH) 3 . MAFL/NAFL involves simple steatosis without notable inflammation or fibrosis and is often viewed as relatively mild, though progression can occur. In contrast, MASH/NASH features steatosis accompanied by inflammation and hepatocellular damage, which may advance to fibrosis, cirrhosis, or even hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) 3 , 4 .
Key contributors to MASLD/NAFLD include obesity, type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, hypertension, dyslipidemia, genetic susceptibility, and unhealthy lifestyle habits 5 , 6 . At present, few medications have been approved in the United States specifically for MASLD/NAFLD or MASH/NASH therapy 5 , 7 . Current management focuses on reducing excess weight through lifestyle modification, pharmacologic therapy, or bariatric and endoscopic procedures, and correcting metabolic abnormalities 8 , 9 . Therefore, a deeper understanding of the molecular pathways driving hepatic lipid accumulation is urgently needed for novel therapy development.
Hepatic steatosis develops when lipid acquisition exceeds lipid disposal—that is, when fatty acid uptake and de novo lipogenesis outpace fatty acid oxidation and lipid export. In MASLD/NAFLD, both hepatic fatty acid uptake and lipogenesis are elevated, whereas the compensatory increase in fatty acid oxidation is insufficient to normalize lipid le

### Plasmid construction
To overexpress METTL7A or SAPCD2, their coding sequence was respectively ligated into the pECMV-3 × FLAG or pLVX-CMV-HA-pGK-puro backbone. The resulting vector was named Flag-METTL7A or SAPCD2 OE. In order to deplete METTL7A, its targeting shRNAs were inserted into the pLKO.1-puro backbone. Three shMETTL7A constructs were produced: shMETTL7A-1, shMETTL7A-2, and shMETTL7A-3. A non-specific shRNA (shNC) was constructed to function as a control. All the resulting plasmids were subjected to Sanger sequencing to ensure sequence accuracy before being used for functional assays. Table 1 shows the details of primers. Plasmid transfection was performed using Lipofectamine® 2000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11668-019) when cells reached 70–80% confluence.

### Quantitative PCR (qPCR)
The RaPure Total RNA Kit (Magen, R4011-02) was employed to extract total cellular and tissue RNA, following the manufacturer’s instructions. Genomic DNA was digested, and RNase-free water was applied to elute RNA. The purified RNA was used for cDNA synthesis using All-in-One First-Strand SuperMix containing dsDNase (Nuoyang Biotech, EG15133S). qPCR was performed using ChamQ SYBR Color qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Q431-02) on a QuantStudio 3 system (ThermoFisher, A28573 ). Relative targeted gene expression was determined based on the 2 –ΔΔCt method, normalizing to 18S. The primers used for qPCR are listed in Table 2 .

### RNA-seq and data analysis
Total RNA was extracted and purified from OA-treated HepG2 cells (shNC or shMETTL7A) using the method described above. For library preparation, 1 µg of RNA per sample was processed with the NEBNext® Ultra™ RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina® (New England Biolabs) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA fragment selection and purification were performed using the AMPure XP system (Beckman Coulter), and library quality was evaluated with the Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100. Clustering of index-coded libraries was carried out on the cBot Cluster Generation System using the TruSeq PE Cluster Kit v3-cBot-HS (Illumina). Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq platform to generate 150 bp paired-end reads. Three independent biological replicates were performed and analyzed for each experimental condition.

### METTL7A expression is upregulated in an MASLD/NAFLD cellular model
To investigate the potential role of METTL7A in MASLD/NAFLD, we first optimized the in vitro steatosis model conditions using a concentration gradient of OA. HepG2 and Huh7 cells were treated with various concentrations of OA for 24 h, and cell viability was evaluated using MTT assays. Based on the cell viability results and the efficiency of intracellular lipid deposition assessed by Oil Red O staining, optimal and non-toxic concentrations of 1 mM for HepG2 cells and 200 μM for Huh7 cells were selected for subsequent experiments, which align with widely used protocols to induce lipid accumulation 23 , 24 . Huh7 cells exhibited cytotoxicity above 200 μM, whereas HepG2 cells maintained high viability up to 1 mM. Both cell lines displayed marked intracellular lipid deposition as detected by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 1 A, B). qPCR and Western blotting revealed significant increases in METTL7A mRNA and protein levels in OA-treated HCC cells compared with controls (Fig. 1 C, D). These results suggest that METTL7A may contribute to lipid accumulation in hepatocytes.

### METTL7A knockdown mitigates lipid accumulation in OA-treated HCC cells
To define METTL7A’s function in hepatic lipid metabolism, we generated three METTL7A-targeting shRNAs. qPCR analysis in HEK293T cells showed effective knockdown by all constructs, with shMETTL7A-1 achieving the greatest suppression (Fig. 2 A); thus, it was selected for further experiments. In both HepG2 and Huh7 cells, METTL7A depletion markedly reduced OA-induced lipid accumulation as shown by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 2 B). MTT assays showed that METTL7A silencing partially rescued the OA-induced decrease in cell viability (Fig. 2 C). Consistent with reduced lipid accumulation, METTL7A knockdown significantly lowered LDL-C, TG, and TC levels while increasing HDL-C in OA-treated cells (Fig. 2 D). At the molecular scale, METTL7A depletion was confirmed by qPCR and Western blotting (Fig. 3 A, B). Moreover, METTL7A deficiency downregulated ACC and FAS expression while upregulating HSL in OA-treated hepatocytes (Fig. 3 B). These findings indicate that METTL7A acts as a positive regulator of lipid accumulation.
METTL7A knockdown reduces lipid accumulation and improves cell viability in OA-treated hepatocytes. ( A ) qPCR validation of three METTL7A-targeting shRNAs in HEK293T cells, identifying shMETTL7A-1 as the most effective construct. ( B ) Oil Red O staining of HepG2 and Huh7 cells with or without METTL7A knockdown following OA treatment. Lipid droplet areas was performed using ImageJ software. ( C ) MTT assay showing that METTL7A depletion partially rescues OA-induced reduction in cell viability. ( D ) Biochemical measurements of LDL-C, TG, TC, and HDL-C levels in control and OA-treated cells with or without METTL7A silencing. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test was used for P-value calculation. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3). Fig. 3.

### Depletion of METTL7A causes reduced expression of PLIN5 and blocks the activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway
To delineate the mechanism by which METTL7A promotes lipid deposition in OA-treated HCC cells, we performed RNA-seq using control and METTL7A-deficient HepG2 cells exposed to OA for 24 h. Among the DEGs, PLIN5 attracted our attention due to its known function in hepatic lipid metabolism. qPCR and Western blotting validated the RNA-seq data, showing that PLIN5 expression was greatly decreased in OA-treated METTL7A-deficient HCC cells. Notably, PLIN5 expression was also strongly induced by OA treatment, similar to METTL7A (Fig. 4 A and B). We also investigated the activation of PI3K/AKT pathway, a key player in hepatic lipid metabolism. Western blotting indicated that the phosphorylation of PI3K and AKT (P-PI3K and P-AKT), which represents activation of the pathway, was enhanced by OA in both cell lines; however, this effect was nullified by METTL7A depletion (Fig. 4 C). These observations demonstrate that METTL7A facilitates lipid accumulation in the hepatocytes by inducing PLIN5 and the PI3K/AKT pathway.

### METTL7A interacts with SAPCD2 in HCC cells
To further explore how METTL7A regulates PLIN5 and PI3K/AKT signaling, a preliminary MS screening was initially performed as an exploratory approach using control and Flag-METTL7A–expressing HepG2 cells, with candidates cross-referenced against PLIN5 interactors in BioGRID 25 . Among the candidates, SAPCD2 emerged as a candidate of interest (Fig. 5 A) because it is also reported to activate PI3K/AKT signaling 26 . Coomassie blue staining of proteins pulled down by IP revealed a potential band corresponding to SAPCD2 (Fig. 5 B). Exogenous co-IP assays verified the interaction between overexpressed METTL7A and SAPCD2 in HepG2 and Huh7 cells (Fig. 5 C). Furthermore, endogenous co-IP assays confirmed that native METTL7A physically interacts with endogenous SAPCD2 under physiological conditions in HepG2 and Huh7 cells (Fig. 5 D). Additionally, qPCR and Western blotting revealed that METTL7A-deficient HepG2 and Huh7 cells exhibited significantly reduced SAPCD2 expression (Fig. 5 E and F). These findings suggest that METTL7A may regulate PLIN5 expression and PI3K/AKT activation in hepatocytes through SAPCD2.

### SAPCD2 is required for OA-induced PI3K/AKT activation and PLIN5 expression
To define the functional role of SAPCD2, we first validated its knockdown and overexpression efficiencies in hepatocytes (Fig. 6 A, B). Western blotting revealed that OA stimulation significantly upregulated METTL7A, SAPCD2, and PLIN5 expression, alongside increased PI3K and AKT phosphorylation. SAPCD2 silencing suppressed OA-induced p-PI3K and p-AKT levels and abolished PLIN5 upregulation without altering METTL7A (Fig. 6 C, D). Conversely, SAPCD2 overexpression further enhanced PI3K/AKT phosphorylation and PLIN5 expression (Fig. 6 C, D). Consistent with these molecular changes, Oil Red O staining demonstrated that SAPCD2 knockdown significantly attenuated OA-induced intracellular lipid accumulation, whereas SAPCD2 overexpression further exacerbated lipid droplet deposition in both cell lines (Fig. 6 E). These results indicate that SAPCD2 acts downstream of METTL7A to mediate OA-induced PI3K/AKT activation and PLIN5 expression.

### Overexpression of SAPCD2 rescues lipid accumulation in OA-treated HCC cells with METTL7A deficiency
To evaluate whether SAPCD2 mediates the lipogenic effects of METTL7A, we overexpressed SAPCD2 in METTL7A-deficient HepG2 and Huh7 cells. SAPCD2 overexpression restored lipid accumulation in OA-treated METTL7A-knockdown cells, as shown by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 7 A). MTT assays indicated that cell viability decreased upon SAPCD2 overexpression in METTL7A-deficient, OA-treated cells (Fig. 7 B). Furthermore, SAPCD2-overexpressing METTL7A-deficient HCC cells expressed higher levels of LDL-C, TG, and TC, along with lower levels of HDL-C (Fig. 7 C). Additionally, qPCR and Western blotting uncovered that overexpression of SAPCD2 significantly increased the expression of PLIN5 in OA-induced METTL7A-deficient HCC cells (Fig. 8 A and B). qPCR also showed that SAPCD2 overexpression led to downregulated levels of HSL and upregulated expression of FAS and ACC (Fig. 8 A). Western blotting indicated that the PI3K/AKT pathway activation was enhanced by excessive SAPCD2 in METTL7A-deficient HCC cells exposed to OA (Fig. 8 B). These data suggest that SAPCD2 is a critical mediator of METTL7A’s role in promoting lipogenesis in OA-treated HCC cells.
SAPCD2 overexpression rescues lipid accumulation in METTL7A-deficient HCC cells. ( A ) Oil Red O staining showing upregulation of lipid accumulation in METTL7A-knockdown HepG2 and Huh7 cells upon SAPCD2 overexpression. Lipid droplet areas was performed using ImageJ software. ( B ) MTT assay showing reduced cell viability when SAPCD2 is overexpressed in METTL7A-deficient, OA-treated cells. ( C ) Biochemical analysis demonstrating increased LDL-C, TG, and TC and decreased HDL-C after SAPCD2 overexpression. One-way ANOVA and Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test were utilized for P -value calculation. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3). Fig. 8.

### METTL7A knockdown alleviates HFD-induced hepatic steatosis in MASLD/NAFLD mice
To validate these findings in vivo, we established a mouse model of MASLD/NAFLD and infected the mice with AAV carrying shNC or shMETTL7A. Compared to the control group, livers from the Model and Model + shNC groups appeared pale, consistent with steatosis, whereas the Model + shMETTL7A group exhibited darker liver coloration, suggesting reduced lipid content (Fig. 9 A). Histological analysis using H&amp;E and Oil Red O staining confirmed that METTL7A knockdown substantially attenuated steatosis (Fig. 9 B and C). Biochemical assays revealed elevated LDL-C, TC, TG, AST, and ALT and reduced HDL-C in the Model and Model + shNC groups, all of which were partially normalized by METTL7A knockdown (Fig. 9 D). qPCR and Western blotting verified efficient METTL7A knockdown in the liver (Fig. 9 E and F). Expression of PLIN5, SAPCD2, FAS, and ACC was reduced, while HSL levels increased upon METTL7A silencing (Fig. 9 E and F). PI3K/AKT activation, elevated in the Model and Model + shNC groups, was markedly suppressed in METTL7A-deficient livers (Fig. 9 F). Collectively, these results demonstrate that METTL7A promotes hepatic lipid accumulation.

### Discussion
In this study, we identify METTL7A as a previously unrecognized regulator of hepatic lipid metabolism and MASLD/NAFLD progression. Although METTL7A is known as an m 6 A RNA methyltransferase implicated in cancer biology and also functions as a thiol methyltransferase in the liver, playing an essential role in drug metabolism, its metabolic functions in hepatocytes have remained unclear. Our findings demonstrate that METTL7A expression is markedly elevated during hepatocellular lipid loading and that METTL7A actively drives steatosis both in vitro and in vivo. These results broaden our understanding of METTL7A’s role in liver physiology.
The mechanism by which lipid accumulation induces METTL7A overexpression in hepatocytes remains unknown. Previous studies show that METTL7A mRNA expression is regulated by several noncoding RNAs, including miR-6807-5p, LINC01123, miR-654-5p, and miR-27a, across different biological contexts 27 – 29 . Notably, these noncoding RNAs also modulate hepatic lipid metabolism and MASLD/NAFLD 30 , 31 , raising the possibility that they may regulate steatosis by targeting METTL7A. Additionally, METTL7A transcription can be influenced by DNA methylation 32 , but whether this mechanism contributes to its increased expression under steatotic conditions remains to be clarified. Importantly, validation of METTL7A upregulation in liver tissues from MASLD/NAFLD patients will strengthen its clinical relevance.
To elucidate the mechanism underlying METTL7A’s lipogenic function in hepatocytes, we performed transcriptomic analyses and identified PLIN5 as a key candidate. PLIN5 is a central regulator of intracellular lipid metabolism, essential for lipid storage and oxidation 33 – 35 . Consistent with METTL7A’s pro-lipogenic role, PLIN5 knockout mice exhibit impaired lipid accumulation in the heart and skeletal muscle and show resistance to MASLD/NAFLD and HCC, whereas PLIN5 overexpression induces cardiac steatosis 20 , 35 . ### Abstract
Methyltransferase-like protein 7A (METTL7A), an m 6 A RNA methyltransferase and thiol methyltransferase enriched in hepatocytes, has been implicated in cancer biology, yet its role in hepatic lipid metabolism and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD) remains unknown. Hepatic steatosis was induced in HepG2 and Huh7 cells using oleic acid (OA). The role of METTL7A was examined through shRNA-mediated knockdown, RNA sequencing, lipid metabolic assays, and rescue experiments. Protein interactions were assessed via mass spectrometry and co-immunoprecipitation. An AAV-shMETTL7A mouse MASLD/NAFLD model was used to validate in vivo relevance. METTL7A expression was significantly upregulated in OA-induced steatotic hepatocytes. METTL7A silencing mitigated lipid accumulation, improved cell viability, reduced LDL-C, TC, and TG levels, and restored HDL-C. Transcriptomic profiling identified PLIN5 as a key downstream target reduced upon METTL7A depletion. Mechanistically, METTL7A knockdown inhibited PI3K/AKT activation and suppressed PLIN5 expression. Mass spectrometry revealed SAPCD2 as a METTL7A-interacting protein, and SAPCD2 overexpression restored lipid accumulation, PI3K/AKT activation, and PLIN5 levels in METTL7A-deficient cells. In vivo, AAV-mediated METTL7A knockdown alleviated hepatic steatosis, normalized serum lipid profiles and liver injury markers, and reduced SAPCD2, PLIN5, FAS, and ACC while increasing HSL expression. METTL7A is a previously unrecognized regulator of hepatic lipid homeostasis that promotes steatosis by sustaining SAPCD2 expression and activating the PI3K/AKT pathway and PLIN5 expression. Targeting METTL7A may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for MASLD/NAFLD.

### Introduction
Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly named nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) refers to a wide range of liver conditions marked by abnormal fat deposition in hepatocytes among individuals who drink little or no alcohol 1 . It has become one of the most prevalent chronic liver disorders worldwide, strongly associated with metabolic dysfunction and affecting roughly 30% of the global population 2 . MASLD/NAFLD is generally classified into two forms: metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver/nonalcoholic fatty liver (MAFL/NAFL) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis/nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (MASH/NASH) 3 . MAFL/NAFL involves simple steatosis without notable inflammation or fibrosis and is often viewed as relatively mild, though progression can occur. In contrast, MASH/NASH features steatosis accompanied by inflammation and hepatocellular damage, which may advance to fibrosis, cirrhosis, or even hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) 3 , 4 .
Key contributors to MASLD/NAFLD include obesity, type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, hypertension, dyslipidemia, genetic susceptibility, and unhealthy lifestyle habits 5 , 6 . At present, few medications have been approved in the United States specifically for MASLD/NAFLD or MASH/NASH therapy 5 , 7 . Current management focuses on reducing excess weight through lifestyle modification, pharmacologic therapy, or bariatric and endoscopic procedures, and correcting metabolic abnormalities 8 , 9 . Therefore, a deeper understanding of the molecular pathways driving hepatic lipid accumulation is urgently needed for novel therapy development.
Hepatic steatosis develops when lipid acquisition exceeds lipid disposal—that is, when fatty acid uptake and de novo lipogenesis outpace fatty acid oxidation and lipid export. In MASLD/NAFLD, both hepatic fatty acid uptake and lipogenesis are elevated, whereas the compensatory increase in fatty acid oxidation is insufficient to normalize lipid le

### Plasmid construction
To overexpress METTL7A or SAPCD2, their coding sequence was respectively ligated into the pECMV-3 × FLAG or pLVX-CMV-HA-pGK-puro backbone. The resulting vector was named Flag-METTL7A or SAPCD2 OE. In order to deplete METTL7A, its targeting shRNAs were inserted into the pLKO.1-puro backbone. Three shMETTL7A constructs were produced: shMETTL7A-1, shMETTL7A-2, and shMETTL7A-3. A non-specific shRNA (shNC) was constructed to function as a control. All the resulting plasmids were subjected to Sanger sequencing to ensure sequence accuracy before being used for functional assays. Table 1 shows the details of primers. Plasmid transfection was performed using Lipofectamine® 2000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11668-019) when cells reached 70–80% confluence.

### Quantitative PCR (qPCR)
The RaPure Total RNA Kit (Magen, R4011-02) was employed to extract total cellular and tissue RNA, following the manufacturer’s instructions. Genomic DNA was digested, and RNase-free water was applied to elute RNA. The purified RNA was used for cDNA synthesis using All-in-One First-Strand SuperMix containing dsDNase (Nuoyang Biotech, EG15133S). qPCR was performed using ChamQ SYBR Color qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Q431-02) on a QuantStudio 3 system (ThermoFisher, A28573 ). Relative targeted gene expression was determined based on the 2 –ΔΔCt method, normalizing to 18S. The primers used for qPCR are listed in Table 2 .

### RNA-seq and data analysis
Total RNA was extracted and purified from OA-treated HepG2 cells (shNC or shMETTL7A) using the method described above. For library preparation, 1 µg of RNA per sample was processed with the NEBNext® Ultra™ RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina® (New England Biolabs) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA fragment selection and purification were performed using the AMPure XP system (Beckman Coulter), and library quality was evaluated with the Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100. Clustering of index-coded libraries was carried out on the cBot Cluster Generation System using the TruSeq PE Cluster Kit v3-cBot-HS (Illumina). Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq platform to generate 150 bp paired-end reads. Three independent biological replicates were performed and analyzed for each experimental condition.

### METTL7A expression is upregulated in an MASLD/NAFLD cellular model
To investigate the potential role of METTL7A in MASLD/NAFLD, we first optimized the in vitro steatosis model conditions using a concentration gradient of OA. HepG2 and Huh7 cells were treated with various concentrations of OA for 24 h, and cell viability was evaluated using MTT assays. Based on the cell viability results and the efficiency of intracellular lipid deposition assessed by Oil Red O staining, optimal and non-toxic concentrations of 1 mM for HepG2 cells and 200 μM for Huh7 cells were selected for subsequent experiments, which align with widely used protocols to induce lipid accumulation 23 , 24 . Huh7 cells exhibited cytotoxicity above 200 μM, whereas HepG2 cells maintained high viability up to 1 mM. Both cell lines displayed marked intracellular lipid deposition as detected by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 1 A, B). qPCR and Western blotting revealed significant increases in METTL7A mRNA and protein levels in OA-treated HCC cells compared with controls (Fig. 1 C, D). These results suggest that METTL7A may contribute to lipid accumulation in hepatocytes.

### METTL7A knockdown mitigates lipid accumulation in OA-treated HCC cells
To define METTL7A’s function in hepatic lipid metabolism, we generated three METTL7A-targeting shRNAs. qPCR analysis in HEK293T cells showed effective knockdown by all constructs, with shMETTL7A-1 achieving the greatest suppression (Fig. 2 A); thus, it was selected for further experiments. In both HepG2 and Huh7 cells, METTL7A depletion markedly reduced OA-induced lipid accumulation as shown by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 2 B). MTT assays showed that METTL7A silencing partially rescued the OA-induced decrease in cell viability (Fig. 2 C). Consistent with reduced lipid accumulation, METTL7A knockdown significantly lowered LDL-C, TG, and TC levels while increasing HDL-C in OA-treated cells (Fig. 2 D). At the molecular scale, METTL7A depletion was confirmed by qPCR and Western blotting (Fig. 3 A, B). Moreover, METTL7A deficiency downregulated ACC and FAS expression while upregulating HSL in OA-treated hepatocytes (Fig. 3 B). These findings indicate that METTL7A acts as a positive regulator of lipid accumulation.
METTL7A knockdown reduces lipid accumulation and improves cell viability in OA-treated hepatocytes. ( A ) qPCR validation of three METTL7A-targeting shRNAs in HEK293T cells, identifying shMETTL7A-1 as the most effective construct. ( B ) Oil Red O staining of HepG2 and Huh7 cells with or without METTL7A knockdown following OA treatment. Lipid droplet areas was performed using ImageJ software. ( C ) MTT assay showing that METTL7A depletion partially rescues OA-induced reduction in cell viability. ( D ) Biochemical measurements of LDL-C, TG, TC, and HDL-C levels in control and OA-treated cells with or without METTL7A silencing. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test was used for P-value calculation. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3). Fig. 3.

### Depletion of METTL7A causes reduced expression of PLIN5 and blocks the activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway
To delineate the mechanism by which METTL7A promotes lipid deposition in OA-treated HCC cells, we performed RNA-seq using control and METTL7A-deficient HepG2 cells exposed to OA for 24 h. Among the DEGs, PLIN5 attracted our attention due to its known function in hepatic lipid metabolism. qPCR and Western blotting validated the RNA-seq data, showing that PLIN5 expression was greatly decreased in OA-treated METTL7A-deficient HCC cells. Notably, PLIN5 expression was also strongly induced by OA treatment, similar to METTL7A (Fig. 4 A and B). We also investigated the activation of PI3K/AKT pathway, a key player in hepatic lipid metabolism. Western blotting indicated that the phosphorylation of PI3K and AKT (P-PI3K and P-AKT), which represents activation of the pathway, was enhanced by OA in both cell lines; however, this effect was nullified by METTL7A depletion (Fig. 4 C). These observations demonstrate that METTL7A facilitates lipid accumulation in the hepatocytes by inducing PLIN5 and the PI3K/AKT pathway.

### METTL7A interacts with SAPCD2 in HCC cells
To further explore how METTL7A regulates PLIN5 and PI3K/AKT signaling, a preliminary MS screening was initially performed as an exploratory approach using control and Flag-METTL7A–expressing HepG2 cells, with candidates cross-referenced against PLIN5 interactors in BioGRID 25 . Among the candidates, SAPCD2 emerged as a candidate of interest (Fig. 5 A) because it is also reported to activate PI3K/AKT signaling 26 . Coomassie blue staining of proteins pulled down by IP revealed a potential band corresponding to SAPCD2 (Fig. 5 B). Exogenous co-IP assays verified the interaction between overexpressed METTL7A and SAPCD2 in HepG2 and Huh7 cells (Fig. 5 C). Furthermore, endogenous co-IP assays confirmed that native METTL7A physically interacts with endogenous SAPCD2 under physiological conditions in HepG2 and Huh7 cells (Fig. 5 D). Additionally, qPCR and Western blotting revealed that METTL7A-deficient HepG2 and Huh7 cells exhibited significantly reduced SAPCD2 expression (Fig. 5 E and F). These findings suggest that METTL7A may regulate PLIN5 expression and PI3K/AKT activation in hepatocytes through SAPCD2.

### SAPCD2 is required for OA-induced PI3K/AKT activation and PLIN5 expression
To define the functional role of SAPCD2, we first validated its knockdown and overexpression efficiencies in hepatocytes (Fig. 6 A, B). Western blotting revealed that OA stimulation significantly upregulated METTL7A, SAPCD2, and PLIN5 expression, alongside increased PI3K and AKT phosphorylation. SAPCD2 silencing suppressed OA-induced p-PI3K and p-AKT levels and abolished PLIN5 upregulation without altering METTL7A (Fig. 6 C, D). Conversely, SAPCD2 overexpression further enhanced PI3K/AKT phosphorylation and PLIN5 expression (Fig. 6 C, D). Consistent with these molecular changes, Oil Red O staining demonstrated that SAPCD2 knockdown significantly attenuated OA-induced intracellular lipid accumulation, whereas SAPCD2 overexpression further exacerbated lipid droplet deposition in both cell lines (Fig. 6 E). These results indicate that SAPCD2 acts downstream of METTL7A to mediate OA-induced PI3K/AKT activation and PLIN5 expression.

### Overexpression of SAPCD2 rescues lipid accumulation in OA-treated HCC cells with METTL7A deficiency
To evaluate whether SAPCD2 mediates the lipogenic effects of METTL7A, we overexpressed SAPCD2 in METTL7A-deficient HepG2 and Huh7 cells. SAPCD2 overexpression restored lipid accumulation in OA-treated METTL7A-knockdown cells, as shown by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 7 A). MTT assays indicated that cell viability decreased upon SAPCD2 overexpression in METTL7A-deficient, OA-treated cells (Fig. 7 B). Furthermore, SAPCD2-overexpressing METTL7A-deficient HCC cells expressed higher levels of LDL-C, TG, and TC, along with lower levels of HDL-C (Fig. 7 C). Additionally, qPCR and Western blotting uncovered that overexpression of SAPCD2 significantly increased the expression of PLIN5 in OA-induced METTL7A-deficient HCC cells (Fig. 8 A and B). qPCR also showed that SAPCD2 overexpression led to downregulated levels of HSL and upregulated expression of FAS and ACC (Fig. 8 A). Western blotting indicated that the PI3K/AKT pathway activation was enhanced by excessive SAPCD2 in METTL7A-deficient HCC cells exposed to OA (Fig. 8 B). These data suggest that SAPCD2 is a critical mediator of METTL7A’s role in promoting lipogenesis in OA-treated HCC cells.
SAPCD2 overexpression rescues lipid accumulation in METTL7A-deficient HCC cells. ( A ) Oil Red O staining showing upregulation of lipid accumulation in METTL7A-knockdown HepG2 and Huh7 cells upon SAPCD2 overexpression. Lipid droplet areas was performed using ImageJ software. ( B ) MTT assay showing reduced cell viability when SAPCD2 is overexpressed in METTL7A-deficient, OA-treated cells. ( C ) Biochemical analysis demonstrating increased LDL-C, TG, and TC and decreased HDL-C after SAPCD2 overexpression. One-way ANOVA and Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test were utilized for P -value calculation. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3). Fig. 8.

### METTL7A knockdown alleviates HFD-induced hepatic steatosis in MASLD/NAFLD mice
To validate these findings in vivo, we established a mouse model of MASLD/NAFLD and infected the mice with AAV carrying shNC or shMETTL7A. Compared to the control group, livers from the Model and Model + shNC groups appeared pale, consistent with steatosis, whereas the Model + shMETTL7A group exhibited darker liver coloration, suggesting reduced lipid content (Fig. 9 A). Histological analysis using H&amp;E and Oil Red O staining confirmed that METTL7A knockdown substantially attenuated steatosis (Fig. 9 B and C). Biochemical assays revealed elevated LDL-C, TC, TG, AST, and ALT and reduced HDL-C in the Model and Model + shNC groups, all of which were partially normalized by METTL7A knockdown (Fig. 9 D). qPCR and Western blotting verified efficient METTL7A knockdown in the liver (Fig. 9 E and F). Expression of PLIN5, SAPCD2, FAS, and ACC was reduced, while HSL levels increased upon METTL7A silencing (Fig. 9 E and F). PI3K/AKT activation, elevated in the Model and Model + shNC groups, was markedly suppressed in METTL7A-deficient livers (Fig. 9 F). Collectively, these results demonstrate that METTL7A promotes hepatic lipid accumulation.

### Discussion
In this study, we identify METTL7A as a previously unrecognized regulator of hepatic lipid metabolism and MASLD/NAFLD progression. Although METTL7A is known as an m 6 A RNA methyltransferase implicated in cancer biology and also functions as a thiol methyltransferase in the liver, playing an essential role in drug metabolism, its metabolic functions in hepatocytes have remained unclear. Our findings demonstrate that METTL7A expression is markedly elevated during hepatocellular lipid loading and that METTL7A actively drives steatosis both in vitro and in vivo. These results broaden our understanding of METTL7A’s role in liver physiology.
The mechanism by which lipid accumulation induces METTL7A overexpression in hepatocytes remains unknown. Previous studies show that METTL7A mRNA expression is regulated by several noncoding RNAs, including miR-6807-5p, LINC01123, miR-654-5p, and miR-27a, across different biological contexts 27 – 29 . Notably, these noncoding RNAs also modulate hepatic lipid metabolism and MASLD/NAFLD 30 , 31 , raising the possibility that they may regulate steatosis by targeting METTL7A. Additionally, METTL7A transcription can be influenced by DNA methylation 32 , but whether this mechanism contributes to its increased expression under steatotic conditions remains to be clarified. Importantly, validation of METTL7A upregulation in liver tissues from MASLD/NAFLD patients will strengthen its clinical relevance.
To elucidate the mechanism underlying METTL7A’s lipogenic function in hepatocytes, we performed transcriptomic analyses and identified PLIN5 as a key candidate. PLIN5 is a central regulator of intracellular lipid metabolism, essential for lipid storage and oxidation 33 – 35 . Consistent with METTL7A’s pro-lipogenic role, PLIN5 knockout mice exhibit impaired lipid accumulation in the heart and skeletal muscle and show resistance to MASLD/NAFLD and HCC, whereas PLIN5 overexpression induces cardiac steatosis 20 , 35 . ### Abstract
Methyltransferase-like protein 7A (METTL7A), an m 6 A RNA methyltransferase and thiol methyltransferase enriched in hepatocytes, has been implicated in cancer biology, yet its role in hepatic lipid metabolism and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD) remains unknown. Hepatic steatosis was induced in HepG2 and Huh7 cells using oleic acid (OA). The role of METTL7A was examined through shRNA-mediated knockdown, RNA sequencing, lipid metabolic assays, and rescue experiments. Protein interactions were assessed via mass spectrometry and co-immunoprecipitation. An AAV-shMETTL7A mouse MASLD/NAFLD model was used to validate in vivo relevance. METTL7A expression was significantly upregulated in OA-induced steatotic hepatocytes. METTL7A silencing mitigated lipid accumulation, improved cell viability, reduced LDL-C, TC, and TG levels, and restored HDL-C. Transcriptomic profiling identified PLIN5 as a key downstream target reduced upon METTL7A depletion. Mechanistically, METTL7A knockdown inhibited PI3K/AKT activation and suppressed PLIN5 expression. Mass spectrometry revealed SAPCD2 as a METTL7A-interacting protein, and SAPCD2 overexpression restored lipid accumulation, PI3K/AKT activation, and PLIN5 levels in METTL7A-deficient cells. In vivo, AAV-mediated METTL7A knockdown alleviated hepatic steatosis, normalized serum lipid profiles and liver injury markers, and reduced SAPCD2, PLIN5, FAS, and ACC while increasing HSL expression. METTL7A is a previously unrecognized regulator of hepatic lipid homeostasis that promotes steatosis by sustaining SAPCD2 expression and activating the PI3K/AKT pathway and PLIN5 expression. Targeting METTL7A may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for MASLD/NAFLD.

### Introduction
Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly named nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) refers to a wide range of liver conditions marked by abnormal fat deposition in hepatocytes among individuals who drink little or no alcohol 1 . It has become one of the most prevalent chronic liver disorders worldwide, strongly associated with metabolic dysfunction and affecting roughly 30% of the global population 2 . MASLD/NAFLD is generally classified into two forms: metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver/nonalcoholic fatty liver (MAFL/NAFL) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis/nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (MASH/NASH) 3 . MAFL/NAFL involves simple steatosis without notable inflammation or fibrosis and is often viewed as relatively mild, though progression can occur. In contrast, MASH/NASH features steatosis accompanied by inflammation and hepatocellular damage, which may advance to fibrosis, cirrhosis, or even hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) 3 , 4 .
Key contributors to MASLD/NAFLD include obesity, type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, hypertension, dyslipidemia, genetic susceptibility, and unhealthy lifestyle habits 5 , 6 . At present, few medications have been approved in the United States specifically for MASLD/NAFLD or MASH/NASH therapy 5 , 7 . Current management focuses on reducing excess weight through lifestyle modification, pharmacologic therapy, or bariatric and endoscopic procedures, and correcting metabolic abnormalities 8 , 9 . Therefore, a deeper understanding of the molecular pathways driving hepatic lipid accumulation is urgently needed for novel therapy development.
Hepatic steatosis develops when lipid acquisition exceeds lipid disposal—that is, when fatty acid uptake and de novo lipogenesis outpace fatty acid oxidation and lipid export. In MASLD/NAFLD, both hepatic fatty acid uptake and lipogenesis are elevated, whereas the compensatory increase in fatty acid oxidation is insufficient to normalize lipid le

### Plasmid construction
To overexpress METTL7A or SAPCD2, their coding sequence was respectively ligated into the pECMV-3 × FLAG or pLVX-CMV-HA-pGK-puro backbone. The resulting vector was named Flag-METTL7A or SAPCD2 OE. In order to deplete METTL7A, its targeting shRNAs were inserted into the pLKO.1-puro backbone. Three shMETTL7A constructs were produced: shMETTL7A-1, shMETTL7A-2, and shMETTL7A-3. A non-specific shRNA (shNC) was constructed to function as a control. All the resulting plasmids were subjected to Sanger sequencing to ensure sequence accuracy before being used for functional assays. Table 1 shows the details of primers. Plasmid transfection was performed using Lipofectamine® 2000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11668-019) when cells reached 70–80% confluence.
